consensus_summary: All four blind responses converge on the same core: 'life'/'the life' symbolizes eternal, divine life (zōē) given by God through Jesus Christ — a saving communion with God begun now and consummated in resurrection — with the definite form 'the Life' widely read as a christological title for Christ himself as source and embodiment of that life (John 14:6; 11:25; 1:4; 1 John 5:11-12). Covenant-blessing/Deuteronomic 'choose life' readings appear only as secondary alternatives.
book_summary: The book identifies 'life (the life)' as covenant existence — specifically 'the life the law produces' — grounding it in Deuteronomy 30:19-20 and Leviticus 18:5 (living by keeping God's statutes), and explicitly flags the common teaching ('Christ Himself, and the eternal life imparted to believers') as the view it departs from. Even John 14:6 and Matthew 7:14 are drawn into this covenantal-legal frame.
consensus_core_identification: 'The life' = eternal/divine life in and through Christ; Christ himself as the personal embodiment and source of that life, received by faith.
book_core_identification: 'The life' = covenant existence — the life produced by keeping the law (Deuteronomic/Levitical covenant obedience).
boundary_disagreement: The book retains covenantal texts (Deut 30:15-20; Lev 18:5) that the consensus treats as a secondary register, but reclassifies the central Johannine/christological occurrences (John 14:6) under the covenant-law category, while the consensus subordinates the covenant texts under the eternal-life-in-Christ category. Each side keeps the other's cases but inverts which category governs them.
material_contradiction: The consensus identifies 'the life' as eternal divine life sourced in the person of Christ and received apart from law-keeping (a point mainstream theology makes explicitly, e.g., Gal 3:21 denies the law can give life); the book identifies it as the life the law produces — covenant existence conditioned on obedience to statutes. These are different referents in the same context and sense: accepting 'life is what the law produces' requires rejecting the consensus identification of 'the life' as Christ himself / eternal life given by grace through faith. The book itself signals this by contrasting its definition with the 'commonly taught' view.
rationale: The book does not merely narrow or sharpen the consensus category; it replaces the central referent. The consensus core is christological-eternal life; the book's core is covenantal-legal existence. The covenant reading does appear in Response A as a listed alternative (Deut 30:15-20; Lev 18:5), so this is not NOVEL — it is a known minority/secondary reading elevated to displace the dominant identification. Because the book's common-view note explicitly sets its definition against the consensus teaching, and because 'life the law produces' cannot be equated with 'eternal life imparted through Christ apart from works of law' without contradiction, DIVERGENT is the correct verdict rather than REFINED. Extensions overlap (both admit Deut 30 and John 14:6 as instances), but the governing identification is swapped.
strongest_objection: One could argue REFINED: the covenantal reading is already present in the consensus responses as a recognized alternative, and the book might intend covenant existence as the substance of what Christ embodies in John 14:6 — i.e., a re-grounding rather than a replacement of the christological reading. Under that harmonizing view, the book merely re-weights which register is primary rather than contradicting the consensus referent. However, the book's own contrast with the 'commonly taught' view and its definitional formula 'the life the law produces' cut against this harmonization.
